Sec. 2.4 Tones (p. 337): "Mikaá is a tonal language, with contrastive high and low, e.g. Ø-kà 'wicker' (C5) and L-ká 'leaf' (C7). The tones may occur singly or in sequences, resulting in high-low and low–high tone sequences, e.g. kâ 'down there' and ... 'eating'. A high tone may be lowered in certain environments, which results in downstep, e.g. ... 'I have seen', or in downdrift. Some morphemes have polar tone, e.g. àlâm 'beloved one' where the tone of the nominalizing prefix a- is opposite to the following tone. Some syllables are analysed as being toneless, e.g. ki 'to go'; if they do not receive a grammatical tone, they receive a default low tone." new_statements.rule_in_words: Both first-hand phonological descriptions (Heath & Heath 1982; Heath 2003) analyse Makaa word prosody exclusively as lexical/grammatical tone (H vs L, contours, floating tones, downstep); neither states a word-stress or accent position, nor explicitly denies stress. The only positional asymmetry noted is distributional: long vowels and labialized/palatalized onsets are confined to the first syllable of the radical (1982: 10-11, 42-43), i.e. the usual NW-Bantu stem-initial prominence, but the authors do not call it stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: toneless syllables get default L; polar-tone prefixes; complex L-HL pattern only word-finally.)
new_statements.domain_note: No stress domain discussed. Tone patterns are stated over the radical in isolation (1982) and the word/verbal complex (2003). Description is of the Mbwaanz dialect (1982 explicitly; 2003 by the same authors).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Heath sources describe the Mbwaanz dialect of Makaa (A83, maka1304), spoken along the Abong-Mbang-Mayos road; Heath 2003 lists four dialects (Mbwaanz, Bibend, Shikunda, Besip) forming a chain with Bikele/Kol (A832) to the south and Byep/North Makaa (A831, byep1241, ISO mkk) to the north - neither of those is covered here. Afane Otsaga 1999 'meka.. du Gabon' may not be this language. Vermeir 2024's accent statement is for Sso (A82), not Makaa.

new_statements.quote: There are two tone levels, /High/ and /Low/, which may occur singly or in sequences. These may combine to form the following tone patterns on radicals in isolation: [Chart 27: Tone Patterns on Noun Radicals] ... Words with more than three syllables have a large number of tone patterns. Rising tone (LH) does not occur on these, and falling tone (HL) occurs only on the final syllable. Underlying tones differ from these surface tones, described above, and underlying tones play a great role, as seen when words are put into context.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makaa (Mbwaanz dialect) is described as a two-level tone language (H, L, plus HL and LH contours on radicals); the phonology has chapters on tone, syllable, radical and phonological word but no section on stress or accent, and the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in the 49-page text (a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned layer). Nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone distribution: LH only on long vowels (and on short vowels in specific morphophonemic contexts such as infinitives); in words of more than three syllables rising tone does not occur and falling tone occurs only on the final syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath & Heath 1982 explicitly describes the Mbwaanz dialect of Makaa (area along the Ndjonkol / Abong Mbang-Mayos road, village of Andjou), chosen as the central and most widely intelligible of the four dialects (Bebend, Mbwaanz, Mpang Sekunda, Besep). Heath 1991 does not name a dialect. Vermeir 2024 (held by the project from an earlier reading) concerns Sso (A82), not Makaa, and its 'Accentuation' section is not about this language.

Since this volume contains descriptions of four of these languages, the extent to which Bantu languages of Zone A mirror the complexities of Grassfields Bantu languages can now be studied more closely. ... new_statements.quote: Makaa has two phonemic tone levels, high (H) and low (L), which are indicated in this paper by accent marks (´ and ` respectively). Long vowels, though written orthographically by a sequence of two vowel symbols, are treated the same as short vowels, since tone appears to function at the syllable level. ... A contour tone is never found on a first syllable, and only the HL contour is found on a final syllable. When disyllabic nouns are spoken in isolation, only the following six tone patterns are found: L-L, L-H, L-HL, H-L, H-H and H-HL.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makaa is treated as a two-level tone language (H, L; HL and LH contours on monosyllables; contour tones never on a first syllable and only HL on a final syllable of disyllabic nouns). The paper is a tone study (spreading, downstep, downdrift, downtilt in the associative construction) and says nothing about word stress; 'accent' occurs only in the sense of tone-marking diacritics. The listed open_url is dead at sil.org (HTTP 404) and the Internet Archive refused connections; the chapter was read from the full-volume scan held by the project.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone-pattern restrictions on disyllabic roots (six surface patterns in isolation, seven underlying); downstep never occurs within a word, only across a word boundary triggered by a floating L.
